2026 — Procedia Computer Science, Vol. 290, pp. 344-351 (Elsevier, open access CC BY-NC-ND), proceedings of the 23rd International Conference on Mobile Systems and Pervasive Computing (MobiSPC), August 18-20, 2026, Athens, Greece (p. 344). Mandatory stratum caveat per PDR-0006/0007: Procedia Computer Science is an A4-stratum conference-proceedings series, below the review's A1-A2/Q1-Q2 quality bar — admissible only under the R1 foundational-conditional rule for secondary studies.

CI/CD pipelines have grown beyond manual human management: failure causes are buried in massive logs, monitoring data overwhelms operators, and AI-generated remediation advice must be validated before deployment (§1, p. 345). Embedding autonomous AI agents in vital pipelines introduces new challenges — hallucination in LLM-based remediation recommendations, non-transparency of automated decisions, and lack of frameworks for securing agent behavior (§1, p. 345). The paper coins 'DevAIOps' for explainable, controllable AI agents in DevOps/DevSecOps workflows affecting KPIs such as MTTR, deployment success rate and security compliance (§1, p. 345), and cites a generative-AI-in-DevOps market of USD 942.5M (2022) projected to USD 22.1B by 2032 at 38.2% CAGR [11] (§1, p. 345). Three RQs cover AI/ML/LLM techniques in CI/CD and AIOps (RQ1), explainability in AI-driven DevOps automation (RQ2), and security risks of LLM-based autonomous remediation, including hallucinations (RQ3) (§1, p. 345).

As an SLR, the paper's contribution is conceptual, not a system: a reproducible review over 217 unique records, a thematic taxonomy over five dimensions (T1 AIOps, T2 AI-driven CI/CD optimization, T3 DevSecOps, T4 XAI in software operations, T5 LLM agents for autonomous software operations), a four-gap analysis, and a research agenda (§1, p. 345; §2.1, p. 346). It motivates a reference DevAIOps architecture (Fig. 1, p. 345) and, for the two trust gaps, proposes a 'trust loop' in which artifact-linked explanations feed OWASP-aligned multi-layer validation and risk-tiered human-in-the-loop gating before any remediation is applied (Abstract, p. 344; Fig. 4, p. 350). The Agentic AI role is synthesized from reviewed primaries: LLM agents (theme T5) for incident RCA, outage summarization and auto-remediation — e.g., ReAct-style tool-using agents [9] — with the proposed research direction of specialized agents for build, security and remediation governed under one explainability layer (Gap 1, §4.1, p. 349).

SECONDARY STUDY — PRISMA-guided SLR (§2, p. 346). Sources: Scopus, Web of Science, plus manually sourced seminal papers; date range January 2019-April 2026, query run 19 April 2026, English only, searched in title/abstract/keywords; example query ('AIOps' OR 'AI-driven DevOps' OR 'CI/CD') AND ('large language model' OR 'LLM agent' OR 'explainable AI' OR 'auto-remediation') (Table 1, §2.1, p. 346). Funnel: 222 candidate publications → 217 unique records → 47 eligible studies → 10 high-impact studies (2019-2025) synthesized in depth (Abstract, p. 344; Fig. 2, p. 347). Ranking used a scripted composite relevance score (0-100) with seven weighted components: citation impact, influential citations, venue quality, recency, open access, tier-1 and tier-2 keywords (Table 2, §2.2, pp. 346-347). Quality assessment used five QA criteria (0/0.5/1.0 each); all ten in-depth studies scored >= 4.0/5.0, seven at the maximum (§2.3, p. 347). Corpus composition: 61% empirical, 26% secondary, 13% conceptual (§3, p. 348). Screening was single-reviewer, partially mitigated by the deterministic scoring algorithm (§5, p. 350).

Secondary evidence only — the review runs no experiment of its own and states that all quantitative figures (such as MTTR decreases) are reported as stated by the original researchers (§5 Conclusion validity, p. 351). MTTR numbers aggregated from reviewed primaries: Zhang et al. [3] (GPT-4 in-context learning for cloud-incident RCA) report 35% higher accuracy than rule-based approaches and a 42% MTTR reduction for RCA in production; Goel et al. [6] (X-Lifecycle, cross-phase attention over SDLC data) report 28% fewer false positives and 31% end-to-end MTTR reduction; Jin et al. [8] report 78% of LLM outage summaries rated helpful by on-call engineers; Roy et al. [9] report 68% top-1 RCA accuracy for a five-tool ReAct agent vs 45% for non-agent methods (§3.5, p. 349). Fu et al. [10] report ML-based runtime anomaly detection reducing incident response time by 65% (§3.3, p. 349). Crucially, the review itself flags (Gap 2) that the 31-55% MTTR improvements in Microsoft studies [3][6][8] rest on proprietary infrastructure, are not externally verifiable, and that no standard MTTR/KPI benchmarks exist (§4.1, pp. 349-350). No MTTD figures are reported anywhere in the paper, and no comparative benefit can be attributed to this paper's own work.

Field: General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Agent Systems
Extraction: The paper names and frames the DevAIOps paradigm — explainable, controllable AI agents inside DevOps/DevSecOps (§1, p. 345) — and maps LLM-agent maturity: theme T5 is among the more mature areas while agent explainability (T4) is the least developed (§3, p. 348; §6, p. 351). For agentic systems specifically it synthesizes that tool-using agents outperform non-agent baselines (68% vs 45% top-1 RCA accuracy, with 12-20% accuracy drop when any of the five tools is removed [9], §3.5, p. 349), and it articulates agent-centric gaps: Gap 1, no unified architecture combining pipeline optimization, security and explainability — proposed as an open-source platform with specialized agents for build, security and remediation under one explainability layer (§4.1, p. 349); Gap 3, explainability exists only at model level, not agent level — ReAct traces are unstructured and not auditable, motivating artifact-linked explanations plus SHAP attribution over agent inputs (§4.2, p. 350); Gap 4, LLM hallucination risk in autonomous remediation is unstudied, aligned with the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic AI Applications (2026) issues of autonomous-action violations, cascading agent failures and unauthorized execution (§4.3, p. 350). The trust loop (Fig. 4, p. 350) — explanations feeding OWASP-based validation and risk-tiered human-in-the-loop gating — is a direct architectural prescription for safe agentic remediation.

Self-reported threats (§5, pp. 350-351): construct validity — keyword/terminological bias despite two-tier terms over five themes; internal validity — single-reviewer screening, only partially mitigated by the deterministic scoring algorithm; external validity — database-coverage bias (Scopus/WoS favored; arXiv-only, non-indexed and grey literature possibly excluded); conclusion validity — quantitative figures taken as reported by original authors, publication bias toward positive findings, and under-representation of 2025-2026 literature. Only 10 of 47 studies received in-depth synthesis due to the conference page limit, and the full 47-study list is available only on request (§2.3, p. 347; §2, p. 346). Future work per gap: an open-source DevAIOps platform with specialized agents under one explainability layer (Gap 1); a multi-dimensional KPI benchmark (MTTR, false fix ratio, test coverage improvement, deployment success rate, security compliance) demonstrated on at least three open-source projects (Gap 2, §4.1, pp. 349-350); a pipeline-native XAI module producing artifact-linked explanations with SHAP attribution (Gap 3, §4.2, p. 350); and measuring hallucination rates of advanced LLMs (GPT-5, Llama 4 Maverick, Mistral Large 3) on real CI/CD failure datasets, with a fix-validation architecture combining static analysis, OWASP Top 10 for LLM and for Agentic AI Applications (2026), and progressive human-in-the-loop gates (Gap 4, §4.3, p. 350).

Directly relevant as a secondary foundational map of the thesis terrain (agentic copilot reducing MTTD/MTTR in incident response): it consolidates the LLM-agent incident-management evidence base the thesis builds on ([3][6][8][9], §3.5, p. 349), confirms MTTR as the paradigm's central KPI while exposing the absence of standardized MTTR benchmarks and the non-verifiability of proprietary results (Gap 2, §4.1, pp. 349-350) — which is precisely the evidence-quality problem the thesis's RSL addresses — and its trust loop with risk-tiered human-in-the-loop gating (Fig. 4, p. 350) matches the copilot (human-supervised) posture the thesis defends over full autonomy. Its gap agenda (unified agent architecture, agent-level explainability, hallucination risk) supplies citable motivation for the dissertation's problem statement. Corpus entry: SECONDARY foundational-conditional study under rule R1 (SLR, no primary evidence of its own), with the mandatory stratum caveat — Procedia Computer Science series, A4 stratum (PDR-0006/0007).

Medium. Thematic alignment is high — LLM agents, auto-remediation, MTTR as explicit KPI and incident-response themes are the review's core — but it contributes secondary evidence only (no own MTTD/MTTR measurement; MTTD never addressed), and it carries the mandatory A4-stratum caveat (Procedia/MobiSPC, PDR-0006/0007), so it supports the thesis's related-work and gap argumentation rather than its empirical base.
